prompt: You want ECS to run nginx with a port, a memory limit and an environment variable. What do you hand ECS?
hint: ECS starts everything from one kind of document.

choices.text: A container you built and saved with docker save
choices.why: ECS never takes a container. It pulls an image by name, as the definition says.

choices.text: A task definition
choices.why: The image, the port, the memory and the environment are fields of one versioned JSON document.

choices.text: A docker run command line, stored in the cluster's settings
choices.why: Clusters store no commands; the flags of docker run become fields of a task definition.

choices.text: An AMI with nginx installed
choices.why: That is how an EC2 instance gets software, lesson 2's subject; ECS runs images, not AMIs.

prompt: The application in a task calls S3 and is refused with AccessDenied. The image was pulled and the logs arrive. Which role needs the S3 permission?
hint: Who is calling S3: ECS, or the code?

choices.text: The execution role, since it already works
choices.why: It works for ECS pulling and logging. The code in the container never receives it.

choices.text: The container instance's role
choices.why: Taking the instance's role from a task is what a hop limit of 1 is there to prevent.

choices.text: The task role
choices.why: It is the role the SDK inside the container finds credentials for, so the code's permissions go on it.

choices.text: Both, because ECS merges the two before the task starts
choices.why: ECS does not merge them: each serves a different caller at a different moment.

prompt: Match each field of web.json to what it decides.
hint: Two are roles, one names revisions, one ties the task's life to a container.

pairs.right: What ECS may do to pull the image and send logs
What the code in the container may call
Whether the task stops when this container stops

prompt: web.json was registered twice, then web:1 was deregistered. What does describe-task-definition --task-definition web return?
hint: A family with no number means one particular revision.

choices.text: Revision 2, the latest ACTIVE one
choices.why: Without a number ECS takes the newest ACTIVE revision, which the capture printed as 2.

choices.text: Revision 1, the first one registered
choices.why: Revision 1 is INACTIVE, and the family alone never means the first.

choices.text: An error, because the family now holds an INACTIVE revision
choices.why: One INACTIVE revision does not stop the others from being described.

choices.text: Both revisions, merged into one
choices.why: Revisions are separate, immutable documents; nothing merges them.

prompt: In a task definition, cpu is counted in units of one ___th of a vCPU, so 256 is a quarter.
hint: A power of two, four times 256.

prompt: A colleague puts the database password in the environment list of a task definition. Who can read it?
hint: Where is a task definition kept, and who can describe it?

choices.text: Only the code in the container, because environment variables are private to a process
choices.why: Inside the container, yes; but the value is also stored in the definition, in plain text.

choices.text: Nobody, because AWS encrypts every task definition
choices.why: AWS stores it, and returns it in clear to whoever may describe it.

choices.text: Anybody allowed to describe the task definition
choices.why: It is a plain field of the document. A secret goes in secrets, a reference the execution role resolves.

choices.text: Only the execution role
choices.why: A role is not a reader of documents; people and programs with ecs:DescribeTaskDefinition are.

prompt: A report runs for twenty minutes every night and exits. How should it run on ECS?
hint: Think about what a service does when its task exits.

choices.text: As a service with a desired count of 1
choices.why: The service would start the report again the moment it finished, all night.

choices.text: As a service with desired 0, raised by hand each night
choices.why: That is run-task with extra steps, and somebody has to remember to lower it again.

choices.text: As an essential container added to the web task
choices.why: Then the report finishing would stop the web task too.

choices.text: As a task started with run-task
choices.why: run-task starts it and forgets it, which is what a job that ends is for.

prompt: A service has a desired count of 6 and maximumPercent 200. How many tasks may exist at once during a deployment?
hint: A percentage of the desired count.

prompt: The same service, desired 6, has minimumHealthyPercent 50. What is the fewest tasks that must keep serving during the deployment?
hint: Half of the desired count.

prompt: In moto, a service asked for 3 tasks reports desiredCount 3, runningCount 0, pendingCount 3, and no task appears. What does it tell you about AWS?
hint: moto keeps the records and runs no scheduler.

choices.text: Nothing: on AWS the scheduler would start three tasks
choices.why: moto stores the service and starts none; the loop that starts and replaces tasks is AWS's.

choices.text: That the cluster has no instances, so AWS would say the same
choices.why: The cluster had a registered instance with room; moto still started nothing.

choices.text: That services wait for a deployment before starting tasks
choices.why: On AWS creating the service is the deployment, and its tasks start right away.

choices.text: That pendingCount means the tasks are queued for a free slot
choices.why: There was a free slot; the pending count is a number moto wrote and never moves.

prompt: A cluster of instances you run has no room for a single extra task, and the service of 4 must deploy a new revision without new instances. Which deployment configuration works?
hint: The maximum caps how many exist at once.

choices.text: minimumHealthyPercent 100, maximumPercent 200
choices.why: That starts new tasks beside the old ones, which needs room for up to 8.

choices.text: minimumHealthyPercent 50, maximumPercent 100
choices.why: Never more than 4 exist, so old tasks stop first and the cluster holds no more than it does today.

choices.text: minimumHealthyPercent 100, maximumPercent 100
choices.why: No task may stop before another starts, and none may start: the deployment cannot move.

choices.text: minimumHealthyPercent 0, maximumPercent 200
choices.why: It allows stopping everything, and still lets ECS start new tasks first, which needs room.

prompt: Which of these does a service do on AWS that the lab's moto did not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare what the commands asked for with what moto showed afterwards.

choices.text: Start tasks until the running count reaches the desired count
choices.why: moto left runningCount at 0.

choices.text: Start a replacement when one of its tasks stops
choices.why: That loop is the service's whole value, and moto has no scheduler to run it.

choices.text: Create a new PRIMARY deployment when the revision changes
choices.why: moto changed the service's revision and kept the old deployment as the only one.

choices.text: Refuse to delete the service while it wants tasks
choices.why: moto refused that too, as AWS does; it is the one rule here it enforced.

choices.text: Edit the task definition revision it runs
choices.why: Nothing edits a revision, on AWS or anywhere: a change is a new revision.

prompt: An instance booted from the ECS-optimised AMI. How does its agent know which cluster to join?
hint: Lesson 7 is the mechanism.

choices.text: From ECS_CLUSTER in /etc/ecs/ecs.config, written by user data
choices.why: Without the line it joins the cluster called default.

choices.text: From the instance's tags, which ECS reads at launch
choices.why: ECS reads no tags to decide membership; the agent reads its configuration file.

choices.text: It joins every cluster in the Region and the scheduler picks
choices.why: A container instance belongs to exactly one cluster.

choices.text: From the subnet it was launched in
choices.why: Clusters are not tied to subnets; the same subnet can hold instances of many clusters.

prompt: A task with hostPort 8080 runs on the cluster's only instance. You start a second copy. What does AWS answer?
hint: moto answered no tasks and no failures; AWS says why.

choices.text: The task starts on port 8081, the next free one
choices.why: ECS does not renumber a fixed port; hostPort 0 is how you ask for any free one.

choices.text: A failure with the reason RESOURCE:PORTS
choices.why: The only instance with room has the port taken, and the scheduler says so.

choices.text: Both tasks share port 8080 and take turns
choices.why: Two processes cannot bind one port on one host, as Docker showed on the laptop.

choices.text: The first task is stopped to make room
choices.why: Placing a new task never stops a running one.

prompt: An m7g.large is 0.1301 USD an hour on the sheet. What does one cost as a container instance for a month of 730 hours, in USD, to the cent?
hint: Hourly price times 730; ECS adds nothing.

prompt: A service's strategy is base=2 on FARGATE, weight 1 on FARGATE and weight 3 on FARGATE_SPOT. With 10 tasks, how many run on FARGATE?
hint: The base first, then the rest divided 1 to 3.

prompt: moto registered the m7i.large with 4,096 CPU units. How many does the ECS agent register for it on AWS?
hint: Two vCPUs, at 1,024 units each.

choices.text: 4,096, as moto said
choices.why: moto's figure is a placeholder; an m7i.large has 2 vCPUs.

choices.text: 2,048, two vCPUs of 1,024 each
choices.why: That is what the agent registers; moto's 4,096 is a placeholder.

choices.text: 1,024, because the agent keeps a vCPU for itself
choices.why: The agent keeps some memory back, not a whole vCPU.

choices.text: 8,192, one unit per MiB of memory
choices.why: CPU units count processor, not memory; 8 GiB is a separate resource.

prompt: Put in order what happens between launching a container instance and its first container starting.
hint: User data runs before the agent can know its cluster.
items: The instance boots from the ECS-optimised AMI
The agent registers the instance with that cluster
ECS places a task by subtracting what it asks for from what is left
The agent starts the task's containers through Docker
trap: Registering before the user data has run puts the instance in the cluster called default.

prompt: The container runs with --cpu-shares 256 and nothing else is running on the machine. How much processor can it use?
hint: Shares only matter when containers compete.

choices.text: A quarter of one vCPU, always
choices.why: That would be a cap, and --cpu-shares is a weight.

choices.text: All of it, since there is no competition
choices.why: A weight divides contended time; alone, the container may use every processor.

choices.text: None until another container gives up time
choices.why: Shares never block a container that is alone.

choices.text: 256 MHz of one core
choices.why: Shares are a relative weight, not a frequency.

prompt: A task's only container has memory 512 and its process grows to 600 MiB. What happens on ECS?
hint: The section called memory the opposite of the CPU setting.

choices.text: The kernel kills it and the task stops with an out-of-memory reason
choices.why: memory is a hard limit, as docker inspect's 536870912 bytes was.

choices.text: It is slowed down until it fits
choices.why: Slowing is what CPU contention does; memory has no slow mode.

choices.text: ECS moves it to an instance with more memory
choices.why: ECS never moves a running task; a service would start a new one after it stops.

choices.text: Nothing, because 512 is only a reservation
choices.why: That is memoryReservation, the soft value; memory is the hard one.

prompt: The port mapping with hostPort 8080 and containerPort 80 becomes the docker run flag -p ___.
hint: Host first, container second.

prompt: The second docker run with -p 8080:80 left web2 in the state Created. Why did it not start?
hint: Read the error Docker printed.

choices.text: The image had to be pulled again
choices.why: The image was already there; the error was about the port.

choices.text: Two containers cannot have the same name
choices.why: They were named web and web2.

choices.text: Port 8080 on the host was already bound by web
choices.why: Docker could not bind it a second time, which is ECS's RESOURCE:PORTS on one machine.

choices.text: Only one container per image may run
choices.why: Any number may run from one image, on different ports.

prompt: A service with hostPort 8080 runs on three container instances, each with plenty of CPU and memory. Its desired count goes from 3 to 4 and the fourth task is never placed. What fixes it without a fourth instance?
hint: The scarce resource is not CPU or memory.

choices.text: Raise the cpu and memory of the task definition
choices.why: The tasks already fit; asking for more makes placement harder, not easier.

choices.text: Set minimumHealthyPercent to 50
choices.why: That shapes deployments; it does not make a port free.

choices.text: Add a FARGATE_SPOT capacity provider with weight 0
choices.why: A weight of 0 sends it no tasks, and the EC2 instances keep their port problem.

choices.text: hostPort 0 behind a target group
choices.why: Each task gets a free port, so one instance can hold several, and the target group follows the ports.

prompt: A service of 4 deploys a new image with minimumHealthyPercent 100 and maximumPercent 200. Put the steps in order.
hint: Room to spare: the new tasks come first.
items: Register a new revision of the task definition
Point the service at it with update-service
Four new tasks start beside the four old ones
The new tasks pass the target group's health check
The four old tasks are stopped
trap: Stopping the old tasks before the new ones are healthy is what a minimum of 100 forbids.
